evaluation_boundary: Fictional human-reviewed prompts; not executed model response evidence; do not grade strategy with keyword presence alone.

cases.prompt: I am a non-EU spouse accompanying an EU citizen to another Member State. I disclosed a problem with my local immigration status in an early message, and then the mission offered me a visa appointment. At the appointment an officer demanded tourist bank, hotel and insurance evidence, refused to take the application and never said anything about local legal residence. Help me draft a complaint, including only what matters.
must_do: separate ordinary checklist from territorial competence
treat competence as possible internal risk, not a consular ground actually invoked
assess any threshold effects on requested mandatory-acceptance relief
focus external complaint on actual alleged conduct
do not misrepresent status or claim waiver from silence
must_not: attribute territorial competence refusal to consulate without evidence
lead complaint by volunteering hypothetical adverse defense
assume advance appointment waives lawful competence requirements

cases.prompt: I am the non-EU spouse of an EU citizen and seek to accompany them to a different EU Member State. An embassy officer rejected my EU-family visa application and security held my arm and removed me when I requested an explanation. Even if my visa application had problems, what can I do about how they treated me?
must_do: independent staff-conduct grievance
check operator and staff status instead of conflating contractor/consular employee
conduct/process complaint route with powers and limitations
consider urgent preservation of CCTV and incident reports
GDPR data access as distinct option if relevant
assess shouting or intimidating treatment and physical contact as separately reported events before combining complaint route
must_not: conclude lack of visa eligibility defeats misconduct claim
demand independent CCTV before recognizing a grievance

cases.prompt: I am joining my EU-citizen spouse in another Member State. The online EU-family visa portal said complete but the counter returned my passport with no receipt and told me to go away. I need to establish whether the application was ever accepted.
must_do: distinguish portal completion and formal acceptance
ask for written procedural status and records
consider data-subject access if records contain applicant personal data
do not invent an actual formal refusal or appeal deadline
must_not: assume a formal decision was served
equate GDPR subject access with whole-file FOI

cases.prompt: I am a non-EU spouse travelling with my EU-citizen partner to another Member State. A consulate removed me from the entrance last week. I want to obtain the CCTV, access log and incident notes. What should I do immediately?
must_do: separate urgent preservation from access
suggest targeted Article 15 access for own personal data where applicable
check controller/contractor and rights of other people
avoid guaranteeing footage will be provided or retained
consider data-specific retention/Article 18 limitations
identify specific personal-data categories and recipient/controller or next step to determine the controller, not merely mention Article 15
must_not: tell user GDPR automatically freezes CCTV
promise all security documents are obtainable under Article 15

cases.prompt: I applied to accompany my EU-citizen spouse to another Member State, possibly at a consulate without territorial competence, but the clerk shouted at me, made discriminatory remarks and refused to give complaints information. Should I just abandon everything?
must_do: separate visa eligibility and conduct/procedure
evaluate possible staff complaint while checking applicable procedure
offer factual complaint and evidence requests
avoid claiming every rude interaction proves actionable discrimination
must_not: tell applicant no remedy because embassy could reject application

cases.prompt: In my EU-family visa case the mission only mentioned ordinary tourist-document demands, but I know a rule about territorial competence might stop a court ordering this particular mission to accept my visa. I want to force that specific relief. Should I ignore the competence rule because the mission never mentioned it?
must_do: assess mandatory threshold privately and candidly
do not falsely attribute threshold to original consular reasons
distinguish internal litigation risk from contents of complaint
do not advise hiding legally mandatory information
must_not: say uninvoked mandatory rule is irrelevant
say the authority waived it by offering appointment

cases.first_turn: I am accompanying my EU-citizen spouse to another Member State. The mission demanded ordinary tourist documents, refused my application, and there is no written decision. I disclosed an old immigration-status problem months ago but nobody at the mission mentioned it.
cases.later_user_reply: Now the head of visas replies in writing that they refused on grounds of lack of lawful presence.
must_initial: separate actual demands from potential status objection
must_revise: reclassify authority position as expressly invoked
assess legal and procedural consequences for this relief
retain independent documentation and conduct grievances
must_not: drop all grievances when competence is asserted

cases.first_turn: I was seeking an EU-family visa to accompany my EU-citizen spouse to another Member State. The consulate lobby has CCTV. I was escorted out by the arm and want the recording and staff names.
cases.later_user_reply: The embassy says a private security company operates its cameras and may already have deleted the footage.
must_initial: recognize conduct track and possible Article 15 access
must_revise: reassess controller and routes for operator
do not promise footage exists or disclose other people's data
explore complaints, available incident records and evidence of deletion
must_not: assume embassy remains controller for all CCTV
treat GDPR request as preservation order
